title: Production-time qualification of individual critical parts

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a way to establish whether each newly manufactured safety-critical part is fit for its intended service using evidence collected during production, linked to validated models of performance. Instead of relying chiefly on a qualification campaign for a particular component and manufacturing process, it would add defensible acceptance decisions for individual parts, with explicit uncertainty about their expected life or failure risk. Qualification would remain tied to specified requirements and operating conditions.

The essential chain runs from manufacturing measurements to the finished part’s material condition, then to its performance in a particular application. Monitoring a process disturbance, identifying a flaw and predicting service life are different capabilities. A signal correlated with defects in one experiment does not by itself establish the condition or lifetime of another individual part. The proposed system would need to connect these stages reliably and account for what its measurements cannot reveal.

Scope synthesis: the broader concept could apply to several manufacturing processes, but the supplied technical evidence concerns metal additive manufacturing, particularly powder bed fusion and directed energy deposition, with attention to nuclear applications. Its central discipline is industrial engineering through manufacturing metrology, reliability and qualification, with substantial contributions from materials science, nondestructive evaluation and uncertainty modeling. Extension beyond the evidenced manufacturing settings remains proposed.

significance.text: If achieved, this capability could substantially change quality assurance for critical components. NIST documents lengthy, expensive and component-specific qualification associated with variable part properties and incomplete standards. Credible evidence about each manufactured part could reduce dependence on repeated qualification campaigns and make acceptance more responsive to actual production outcomes. The supplied evidence does not quantify the savings or establish that this reduction has occurred.

The direct advance would be justified confidence in individual-part fitness: an acceptance decision supported by measured condition, application-specific performance models and known uncertainty. This could help distinguish acceptable variation from consequential defects. Its value would depend on the decision being reliable enough for the intended service, rather than simply producing more sensor data or more precise-looking predictions.

Conditional downstream synthesis: easier qualification could make production of qualified designs near their point of use more practical, including replacement components made at additional sites. That possibility still requires suitable equipment, controlled materials and processing, applicable standards, and acceptance by the relevant authorities. It would not make a design transferable to arbitrary machines or remove the need to qualify manufacturing processes. No supplied evidence establishes decentralized deployment, universal transferability or actual adoption.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing measurement capability is reliable observation of the manufacturing features that determine final performance. Measurements must reveal relevant defects and material variations, including structural and microstructural evolution. NIST’s 2026 workshop introduction identifies a lack of reliable, validated in-situ measurements of that evolution as a barrier. Sensor coverage and interpretation must therefore be assessed against the properties that matter in service, rather than against anomaly detection alone.

The missing predictive capability is a validated connection between production observations, final-part condition and application-specific performance. NIST’s 2024 report describes incomplete cause-and-effect relationships between process anomalies and part flaws. It also explains that flaws observed during production can change or disappear before manufacturing is complete. Even successful detection of a final flaw leaves a further question: whether its characteristics are acceptable under the part’s intended loads and environment, and what they imply for life or failure risk.

Engineering requirements synthesized from these gaps include bounding the consequences of unobserved features and maintaining defensible uncertainty across qualified machines, sites, geometries and operating conditions. A model must recognize when changed conditions place a part outside its validated capability envelope. These are requirements for the proposed breakthrough, not demonstrated transfer capabilities or verbatim prescriptions from NIST.

Qualification also requires an adequate basis for acceptance: specified end-use requirements, meaningful confidence bounds and evidence that the measurement and prediction methods support the intended decision. NIST identifies gaps in knowledge, technologies and standards that prevent monitoring and nondestructive evaluation from serving as robust qualification tools. Resolving those gaps would require coordinated progress in measurements, material-performance relationships, validation methods and application-specific acceptance practices.

current_state.text: NIST IR 8538, published on September 17, 2024, documents existing uses and ongoing investigation of in-process monitoring and nondestructive evaluation for metal additive manufacturing. It also reports that these methods were not then relied on as the principal sources of qualification evidence for mission-critical applications. This establishes a technical foundation and a documented qualification gap at the report’s date; it does not demonstrate individual-part lifetime prediction or show that the field remained unchanged afterward.

The supplied review had only a partial text extraction of the NIST report, ending during PDF page 43. The earlier citation to page 80 was therefore outside the retained text. The report’s abstract, executive summary and introductory material independently support the statements here about qualification gaps, application-dependent acceptance, uncertainty and incomplete links between process observations and final properties. The extraction limit restricts what can be attributed to the reviewed material; it is not evidence against the unretained portions.

The introduction to NIST’s Roadmapping In-Situ Metrology for Metal Alloy Additive Manufacturing workshop, scheduled for April 29–May 1, 2026, identifies reliable, validated measurements of structural and microstructural evolution as a continuing barrier. The supplied review retained the full event page. That page is an announcement with introductory framing and an agenda, rather than proceedings, workshop findings or a completed roadmap; it supports the stated barrier without establishing the workshop’s outcomes.

The earlier research associated DARPA’s Structures Uniquely Resolved to Guarantee Endurance, or SURGE, program with a goal of predicting individual-part life from manufacturing data. However, the supplied source index contains no captured DARPA text, and the review could not inspect the page or verify that description. The attribution remains provisional. Even if confirmed, a program goal would describe intended research rather than establish successful qualification or life prediction.

Evidence-bound synthesis: the supplied material establishes dated technical foundations and unresolved challenges, but contains no verified demonstration of the complete proposed capability. It also lacks a comprehensive update establishing the field’s status as of November 1, 2026. That absence limits conclusions about later developments; it does not show that additional results do not exist.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independent teams would manufacture several safety-critical part families across qualified machine types and sites within a stated capability envelope. The evaluation would include deliberately introduced faults and geometries unseen during model development but still within that envelope. Before destructive testing or disclosure of reference results, the system would issue acceptance decisions and calibrated life or failure-risk estimates for individual parts.
completion_criteria.label: Blind individual-part acceptance decisions and calibrated life or failure-risk estimates

completion_criteria.text: Proposed validation: subsequent inspection, destructive examination where appropriate, and service-representative testing would assess both the inferred condition and predicted performance. The evidence would need to distinguish detecting an anomaly, identifying a final flaw, deciding whether that flaw is acceptable and estimating its consequences in service. This staged evaluation would address the incomplete process-to-flaw and flaw-to-performance connections documented by NIST, while preserving the requirement for objective evidence with known uncertainty.
completion_criteria.label: Staged validation connects inferred flaws to acceptability and service consequences

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and risk criteria: the protocol would specify application-dependent risk targets, calibration tolerances, sample sizes and methods for evaluating rare failures before testing begins. It would examine incorrect acceptances and unnecessary rejections, the reliability of uncertainty estimates, and whether the system rejects or defers decisions outside its validated envelope. These are proposed design requirements, not established numerical standards; the supplied record does not resolve suitable thresholds or the evidence needed for rare-event assurance.
completion_criteria.label: Predeclared risk protocol evaluates decision errors and uncertainty reliability

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: independent authorities would judge whether the evidence is adequate for each intended application, including its materials, machines, part families and service conditions. Reproduction across teams and sites would demonstrate breadth within those boundaries. A finite test campaign could not establish literal universality, and success would not require certifying arbitrary parts made on arbitrary machines.
completion_criteria.label: Authorities judge evidence adequacy within application boundaries reproduced across sites

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — IND-01, General-purpose, rapidly reconfigurable production: flexible production could benefit from faster, credible qualification when changing designs or production settings. IND-01 concerns the ability to make varied products; IND-02 concerns evidence that each critical part meets its intended requirements. Manufacturing flexibility alone does not establish part fitness, and IND-02 could also be valuable in dedicated production lines.

Roster-based synthesis — IND-03, A predictive and testable science of supply-network cascade containment: qualified production at additional sites could conditionally provide more options during supply disruptions. IND-03 addresses how failures propagate through networks and how to contain them; IND-02 addresses the fitness of individual manufactured parts. Better part qualification would not by itself establish network resilience.

Roster-based synthesis — IND-04, Economical mixed-product disassembly and recovery: both concepts involve decisions under uncertainty about physical materials and components. IND-04 concerns economical separation and recovery from mixed products. IND-02 concerns acceptance and performance assurance for newly manufactured critical parts. Applying its methods to recovered materials or reused components would require additional validation beyond the supplied evidence.

Roster-based synthesis — IND-05, Transferable prediction and prevention of work-related human performance risk: both concepts require risk estimates that remain credible when conditions change. Their prediction targets differ: IND-05 concerns human performance in work settings, while IND-02 concerns manufactured-part condition and service performance. Their overlap is methodological rather than evidence that either capability transfers directly to the other domain.

Roster-based synthesis — IND-06, Transferable safety constraints built into socio-technical systems: individual-part qualification could provide evidence used by broader safety controls. IND-06 concerns constraints across interacting people, organizations and technologies; IND-02 provides a narrower manufacturing assurance capability. Accepting a part for specified service would not establish the safety of the entire system in which it operates.

unresolved_issues: The supplied record cannot verify the DARPA SURGE page’s identity, wording or individual-part life-prediction goal because no source text was captured.
The NIST report extraction is partial, and the earlier page-80 reference cannot be assessed from the retained text.
The workshop announcement does not establish whether a completed roadmap, proceedings or subsequent validation results were produced.
The supplied evidence does not establish comprehensive field status as of November 1, 2026, or resolve whether later demonstrations achieved additional capabilities.
An executable demonstration still requires application-specific numerical risk targets, calibration tolerances, sample sizes and a defensible method for evaluating rare failures.
Transfer across manufacturing processes, machine types, sites, geometries and service conditions remains to be demonstrated within explicit boundaries.
The magnitude of qualification savings, practical point-of-use deployment benefits and regulatory acceptance remains unestablished.

brief.title: Individual checks of critical parts as they are made
possible: A manufacturer could judge whether each newly made critical part is fit for its intended use using measurements taken while making it. Those measurements would support an estimate of its working life or chance of failure, with explicit uncertainty, under specified operating conditions.
why: Manufacturers could rely less on lengthy, expensive qualification campaigns that establish whether a particular component and manufacturing process meet requirements. Decisions about individual parts could distinguish harmless variation from defects that matter in service.
Easier qualification could also make it more practical to produce replacement parts near where they are needed.

sources.who: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sources.showed: The authors reviewed methods for monitoring metal 3D printing and inspecting parts without damaging them. They identified gaps in knowledge, technology and standards that prevent these methods from reliably establishing fitness for use.
sources.cited_for: The report explains why production measurements alone cannot yet justify accepting an individual critical part.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate a complete link from production measurements to reliable decisions about a part's working life or failure risk.

sources.who: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sources.showed: The workshop announcement identifies a shortage of reliable, validated measurements of how metal's internal structure changes during printing.
sources.cited_for: It identifies a measurement gap that limits connections between manufacturing conditions and finished-part performance.
sources.not_established: The announcement does not demonstrate a validated measurement system or successful qualification of individual parts.

sources.showed: This is a research program provisionally associated with predicting individual-part life from manufacturing data.
sources.cited_for: It provides a provisional example of research aimed at predicting individual-part life.
sources.not_established: A research goal does not demonstrate accurate life predictions or reliable decisions about accepting parts.

shown: Metal 3D printing already uses production monitoring and inspection tools. NIST's review documents this foundation, with attention to nuclear components; it reports that these tools were not then the main basis for accepting parts for mission-critical use.
missing: Reliable measurements must capture the defects and material variations that determine performance, including features sensors may miss.
Validated models must connect production signals to the finished part's condition, then to its life or failure risk in its intended use.
The complete system must demonstrate defensible individual-part decisions, including when changed conditions require it to defer a decision.

milestones.label: Blind decisions and reliable predictions for individual parts
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to predict acceptance and life or failure risk before reference results, across approved machines, sites and part families, including planted faults and unfamiliar shapes. This would test individual-part judgment.

milestones.label: Tests connect flaws to performance in use
milestones.explanation: Inspection, destructive examination where appropriate and tests resembling service would have to confirm flaws, their acceptability and predicted consequences. This would connect manufacturing observations to performance.

milestones.label: A declared risk protocol tests errors and uncertainty
milestones.explanation: A protocol set before testing would have to define risk targets and assess rare failures, wrong decisions, uncertainty and deferral outside validated conditions. This would establish how reliability is judged.

milestones.label: Authorities accept evidence reproduced across teams and sites
milestones.explanation: Independent authorities would have to judge evidence adequate for specified applications, with results reproduced across teams and sites. This would establish where the method can support acceptance.

uncertain: Suitable risk targets, prediction tolerances and sample sizes remain unresolved, especially for very rare failures.
How far the method can transfer across manufacturing processes, machines, shapes and service conditions remains open.
The size of any qualification savings and the practical benefits of producing parts near their point of use remain unknown.

page.title: Individual-part qualification in metal additive manufacturing
page.definition: Individual metal parts made by additive manufacturing, which builds material layer by layer, are accepted for specified service using production measurements and validated predictions of their own fatigue life, with quantified uncertainty. Fatigue life counts load cycles to a defined damage endpoint.

goal.need: Qualifying a metal printing process on one machine can take months or years of testing and cost millions of dollars. Even a specimen printed alongside a critical part can have a different fatigue life. If manufacturers could assess the part itself as they make it, more suppliers could produce critical parts where they are needed, including when defence demand rises. That flexibility depends on evidence that the predictions hold across the machines, materials and service conditions involved.

statements.body: Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, SURGE programme
statements.quote: the life of every unique part is predicted at the point of production based directly on data captured during manufacturing.
statements.context: SURGE proposes individual-part life prediction as an alternative approach to machine-centred qualification.

statements.body: National Institute of Standards and Technology, Qualification for Additive Manufacturing Materials, Processes, and Parts
statements.quote: The long range goal of part qualification is the concept of “qualify as you go.”
statements.context: NIST includes measurements before, during and after manufacture as evidence that an individual part will meet its specifications. Fatigue life is one possible performance requirement within that broader goal.

completion.title: A qualification authority accepts critical metal parts using individual production-data-based life predictions.
completion.criterion: A responsible qualification authority authorises a method for accepting individual fatigue-critical metal additively manufactured parts for specified service, relying principally on each part's production measurements and validated fatigue-life prediction with quantified uncertainty. At least one part is accepted under that method. The approval specifies the material, manufacturing and post-processing conditions, geometry, service loads, environment and acceptance requirements within which the method applies.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback, bounded by the qualification goals and application-specific acceptance described in the cited documents.
completion.basis: Searches of SURGE requirements, ASTM E3353-22, AIA's 2025 certification guidance, NIST IR 8538 and the 2026 CM4QC strategy found no end-to-end acceptance test for production-data-based individual-part qualification. SURGE specifies research metrics; CM4QC leaves detailed model acceptance criteria to further regulator engagement. This fallback therefore requires documented acceptance for a specified service.

milestones.title: Build data locate ≥90% of defects larger than 25 µm and predict mean grain size within 50%.
milestones.criterion: In <24 h after the build, reconstruct defects and microstructure on a standard engineering workstation from build measurements alone. Compare with independent measurements of the same volume, at least 1 cm × 1 cm × 0.5 cm, using a method sensitive to 25 µm defects. Predict ≥90% of observed defects larger than 25 µm by major diameter (length for cracks). Figure 2 allows a position error ≤5 major diameters. Predict mean grain size within 50% across ≥3 regions spanning the finest and coarsest grains. Assess build and transverse orientations in each region and report both axes for grains with aspect ratio >2:1.
milestones.set_by: DARPA SURGE, Phase 1 reconstruction demonstration at month 10. The detection fraction is relative to the experimental baseline.

milestones.title: Predicted fatigue life is within 30% of measured life for ≥9 in 10 coupons per condition.
milestones.criterion: Test ≥10 specimens per condition to a defined fatigue endpoint. For ≥9 in 10, the mean of that specimen’s uncertainty-quantified prediction must be within 30% of its measured life. At fixed loading, test four build conditions spanning a ≥5-fold range in maximum defect size. At one build condition, test four load conditions spanning a ≥100-fold range in median life. Meet Phase 1 reconstruction and life-prediction accuracy and timing limits for DARPA-selected conditions on two machines with distinct serial numbers and with the same nominal alloy from two feedstock suppliers.
milestones.set_by: DARPA SURGE, Phase 1 experimental validation and transfer demonstration, month 21 after contract award.
milestones.threshold_quote: within 30% for at least nine (9) out of ten (10) tests conducted.

milestones.title: Independent testing reproduces individual component-life predictions within 40% across two alloys.
milestones.criterion: Validate two DARPA challenge designs and reproduce the workflow externally on ≥1 machine across two alloys. Require ≥9/10 mean life predictions within 40%, ≥10 parts/condition, <12 h from build completion, mean crack-location error ≤5 mm and matching failure-initiating microstructural features. Cover three process conditions and three loading conditions producing initiation sites >20 mm apart. The March 2026 CM4QC review reported no major SURGE outcomes at its publication.
milestones.set_by: DARPA SURGE, Phase 2 challenge-part and independent verification and validation requirements.
milestones.threshold_quote: successfully reproduce performer results on their machines

milestones.title: A transferable sensor package records the build data needed to map defects and microstructure.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate a standalone sensor package during a metal additive build. Collect the measurements needed to model the part’s defects and microstructure. The package must be transferable between machines, and its installation must preserve normal machine operation.
milestones.set_by: DARPA SURGE, Phase 1 sensor demonstration, month 5 after contract award.
milestones.threshold_quote: a sensor suite capable of capturing data during AM to inform the DMT.

milestones.title: A model predicts an individual test specimen’s fatigue life with quantified uncertainty in <12 h.
milestones.criterion: Use the specimen’s reconstructed defects and microstructure to predict its fatigue life under specified loading. Account for competing sites of failure and quantify uncertainty from model assumptions and variable inputs. Run the life calculation on a standard engineering workstation in <12 h after reconstruction, excluding one-time training or calibration.
milestones.set_by: DARPA SURGE, Phase 1 coupon prediction demonstration, month 14 after contract award.

milestones.title: A draft technical specification covers the complete individual-part life-prediction method.
milestones.criterion: The development team and government stakeholders draft a technical specification covering the complete method from measurement during the build through prediction of the individual part’s fatigue life.
milestones.set_by: DARPA SURGE, Phase 2 technical specification, month 45 after contract award.
milestones.threshold_quote: draft a technical specification(s) covering the complete method for life prediction.

milestones.title: On two challenge designs, predicted fatigue life is within 40% for ≥9 in 10 parts per condition.
milestones.criterion: For each DARPA design, the development team tests ≥10 parts per condition. Within <12 h of build completion, including reconstruction, predict each part’s life with quantified uncertainty. The mean prediction must be within 40% of measured life for ≥9 in 10. Mean error in the fatal crack’s initiation site must be ≤5 mm, and fracture-surface examination must confirm the predicted initiating feature. Test low-, medium- and high-quality builds at fixed loading. Vary load direction and amplitude across three load conditions to produce three initiation sites >20 mm apart.
milestones.set_by: DARPA SURGE, Phase 2 performer tests of the first and second challenge designs, months 33 and 39 after contract award.
milestones.threshold_quote: Mean MBL prediction within 40% of experimentally measured life

milestones.title: An independent team reproduces the component-life and crack-initiation tests across two alloys.
milestones.criterion: At an external verification and validation facility, transfer the sensors and software and train the independent team. That team must reproduce the workflow from sensor placement through life prediction on ≥1 of its own machines, using two alloys with distinct Unified Numbering System designations. It builds and tests parts there against the Phase 2 limits: <12 h from build completion, mean life within 40% for ≥9 in 10 parts per condition with ≥10 tested, mean crack-site error ≤5 mm, and agreement on the feature that initiated failure.
milestones.set_by: DARPA SURGE, Phase 2 independent transfer assessment, month 42 after contract award.
milestones.threshold_quote: successfully reproduce performer results on their machines

not_found: No public demonstration satisfying all SURGE coupon, challenge-part and independent-transfer metrics was located.
No published authority decision accepting the complete production-data-based qualification method for a critical metal part was located.
No statement opposing the goal or judging it infeasible was located in DARPA, NIST, AIA or NASA–FAA qualification guidance.

results.detail: The contact image sensor was integrated directly into the recoater blade on the single machine studied.
results.quote: Both images were acquired at a pixel size of 21 µm.

results.finding: For 20 AlSi10Mg specimens, the dual-stream model reached 90% pore detection at about 110 µm equivalent diameter.
results.detail: Test data were held-out layer regions within the specimens. Positive patches were centered on CT-identified pores, and the paper illustrates regular-grid prediction on one layer.
results.quote: Probability of detection analysis showed reliable detection of pores above approximately 110 µm.

results.finding: Single-track LPBF Ti-6Al-4V mean grain-size predictions achieved 93.03% mean agreement across scan speeds. Specimen count unreported.
results.detail: Agreement is 100% minus absolute relative error. The validation compares melt-pool averages across scan speeds.
results.quote: Validation against experimental data demonstrated a mean agreement of 93.03% for grain size prediction across scanning speeds, reaching 97.01% at the industrially relevant 600 mm/s.

results.finding: For one laser powder bed fusion 316L specimen, a model informed by post-build scans predicted a mean crack-initiation life of about 40,400 cycles.

results.finding: For four AMBench Ti-6Al-4V rotating-bending specimens, U-Net segmentation and CT-based pore ranking correctly identified the fatigue-initiating pore in 4 of 4.
results.detail: All three thresholding methods missed the same small near-surface initiating pore. The reported roughly 30 minutes per CT scan covers U-Net inference alone.
results.quote: The 2.5D U-Net was able to predict the fatigue-initiating pore in all four cases despite having a lower Dice coefficient and IoU values when compared to the other segmentation models.

goal.need = "Qualifying a metal printing process on one machine can take months or years of testing and cost millions of dollars. Even a specimen printed alongside a critical part can have a different fatigue life. If manufacturers could assess the part itself as they make it, more suppliers could produce critical parts where they are needed, including when defence demand rises. That flexibility depends on evidence that the predictions hold across the machines, materials and service conditions involved.". Reason: The current paragraph gives the cost of qualification but omits who could use local production, why coupon testing falls short, and what limits transfer to another machine.

add statement by National Institute of Standards and Technology, Qualification for Additive Manufacturing Materials, Processes, and Parts, 2014, updated 2025: "The long range goal of part qualification is the concept of “qualify as you go.”". Reason: NIST’s qualification project explicitly names the part-level goal and explains which measurements it encompasses.

add not found: "No statement opposing the goal or judging it infeasible was located in DARPA, NIST, AIA or NASA–FAA qualification guidance.". Reason: The published reservations concern validation and regulatory acceptance, leaving the question of institutional opposition unanswered.

add milestone after None: "A transferable sensor package records the build data needed to map defects and microstructure.". Reason: SURGE calls for a working sensor package before it tests the accuracy of a reconstructed part.

edit m1: title = "Build data locate \u226590% of defects larger than 25 \u00b5m and predict mean grain size within 50%."; criterion = "In <24 h after the build, reconstruct defects and microstructure on a standard engineering workstation from build measurements alone. Compare with independent measurements of the same volume, at least 1 cm \u00d7 1 cm \u00d7 0.5 cm, using a method sensitive to 25 \u00b5m defects. Predict \u226590% of observed defects larger than 25 \u00b5m by major diameter (length for cracks). Figure 2 allows a position error \u22645 major diameters. Predict mean grain size within 50% across \u22653 regions spanning the finest and coarsest grains. Assess build and transverse orientations in each region and report both axes for grains with aspect ratio >2:1."; set_by = "DARPA SURGE, Phase 1 reconstruction demonstration at month 10. The detection fraction is relative to the experimental baseline."; threshold_quote = "Average grain size within 50%"; threshold_ref = 5; refs = [5]. Reason: The existing criterion includes a preprint result and omits the strict time limit, same-volume comparison and required sampling of the finest and coarsest grains.
